answer: Increased time preference leads to higher Body Mass Index (BMI). Longitudinal evidence from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth demonstrates that individuals exhibiting behaviors indicative of high time preference (present bias/dis-saving or having no savings) exhibit significantly higher subsequent BMI and greater longitudinal BMI gains between 1981, 1989, and 1992 relative to forward-looking individuals who actively save, even after controlling for baseline BMI, cognitive ability (ASVAB), household income, parental education, class standing, demographic characteristics, and longitudinal incarceration history.

payload.hypothesis: Increased time preference leads to higher Body Mass Index (BMI). Individuals with high time preference (evidenced by dis-saving or having no savings) experience significantly higher subsequent BMI and greater longitudinal weight gain over time than those with low time preference (who put more money into savings), even after adjusting for baseline BMI, cognitive test scores, household income, parental education, high school rank, demographic background, and incarceration history.
payload.workflow:
1. Decoded 1981 height from feet-inch notation and combined with 1985 height in inches; cleaned weight measures by removing topcoded/refusal codes (996.0).
2. Computed BMI at 1981, 1989, and 1992, and longitudinal change metrics (Delta BMI 1981-1989 and 1981-1992).
3. Operationalized time preference via 1989 savings behavior (Put more in [low time preference reference], Took out, No change, No savings) and secondary net wealth proxies.
4. Operationalized academic performance using ASVAB standardized four-test composite score and high school percentile class rank.
5. Operationalized incarceration history combining pre-1980 criminal sentencing and longitudinal residence in Jail across 1981-1996 waves.
6. Estimated multivariable OLS regression models with HC1 robust standard errors across cross-sectional, longitudinal lagged-outcome, change-score, and sensitivity specifications.
